entries.title: Share a game of peekaboo
entries.summary: Play a little peekaboo together, leaving time for your baby’s look, sound, or gesture in reply.
entries.cue: Your baby is interested when someone disappears briefly and comes back.
detail: The authors include peekaboo among the games in their 9–12-month language section. Enjoy the back-and-forth and follow the response your baby gives.
A look, a movement, or a sound can be part of the exchange. There is no word your baby has to say to take part.

entries.title: Listen for a sound in the room
entries.summary: Clap from a different place in the room and notice whether your baby turns or moves toward the sound.
entries.cue: A familiar sound makes your baby look around.
detail: The authors suggest playful sounds from different places, including clapping or a rattle. A clap needs no extra material.
Notice what your baby does, then let their interest guide whether you repeat the game.

entries.title: The book’s push-wagon example
entries.summary: For a baby already cruising along furniture, the authors describe a stable push wagon the baby approaches, pulls up on, and pushes by their own choice.
entries.cue: Your baby is cruising and choosing where to move next.
detail: The main discussion waits for cruising to become more efficient. The baby chooses when to approach the wagon and use its handle; the adult does not place them in a supported standing position.
The authors distinguish this push wagon from a seated baby walker. They emphasize a wagon that does not tip when the baby pulls up, and describe slowing its movement while the child is unsteady.
The monthly summary says “once they can pull themselves up,” while the fuller passage adds cruising. The fuller readiness description remains part of this example.

entries.title: Follow a ball down the ramps
entries.summary: The authors describe a ball tracker with ramps to watch and a ball to retrieve. Their standing example requires a large, stable support, with a ball and parts suitable for mouthing.
entries.cue: Your baby watches a moving ball or wants to drop it and find it again.
detail: In the body example, the baby pulls up, drops the ball, bends to retrieve it, and repeats. Watching the ball is also part of the interest.

The appendix lists the activity from creeping, around 8 to 10+ months; it does not require every baby to use the standing version. The authors choose activities by the baby’s current movement and interest.

entries.title: Exploring stairs with an adult
entries.summary: The authors describe supervised stair exploration for a baby who is crawling and interested in climbing. Coming down may need more time and an adult’s modeling.
entries.cue: Your baby is trying to crawl up a step or another low change in level.
detail: They notice that going up can come before knowing how to get down. The monthly table describes showing backward descent.
The appendix’s stair material is a separate example: low, wide steps and a railing at either end of a bridge, listed from creeping until walking well.

entries.title: Post a ball, then find it
entries.summary: The authors describe a posting box whose ball is found by opening a drawer, using one hand to open and the other to retrieve. The ball and every part need to be suitable for mouthing.
entries.cue: Your baby is releasing objects deliberately and looking for where they have gone.
detail: Unlike a box with an open tray, the drawer keeps the ball out of view until the baby opens it. The baby can repeat the part that interests them.
The appendix also describes a knitted-ball version with an opening slightly smaller than its soft ball. This adds pushing the ball through before retrieving it.

entries.title: Exploring a material that changes shape
entries.summary: The authors describe pressing and squeezing pliable materials in their 9–12-month section. For play dough, they describe stopping and trying later if the baby keeps eating it.
entries.cue: Your baby is using thumb and fingers to squeeze, press, or pull.
detail: Their examples include play dough, tissue paper to tear, and squeezable bath toys, within their broader requirement for suitable materials and secure components.
For dough, the authors describe showing a press on the table or a squeeze in the fist. If eating continues, they put the activity aside and try again after a few weeks.

entries.title: A drawer they can investigate
entries.summary: As a baby becomes steadier on their feet, the authors describe an accessible drawer with a few suitable things the adult is happy for them to take out, in a secured space.
entries.cue: Your baby is opening drawers or investigating what is inside.
detail: This gives an ordinary household interest a place. The appendix describes room-related objects, such as kitchen pots and pans, in a cupboard or drawer selected for the baby.
The surrounding movement guidance keeps unsafe cupboards secured and furniture fixed against falling. The objects still need to meet the book’s mouthing, finish and secure-parts conditions.

entries.title: Choosing when the music plays
entries.summary: Junnifa describes her babies choosing to start and pause music with a reachable player button. It is a personal example of choice, alongside the authors’ preference for quiet between musical moments.
entries.cue: Your baby is interested in starting or stopping a familiar sound.
detail: When her babies were around 8 or 9 months, Junnifa marked the play button of a small CD player. They could approach it and later press the same button to pause.
This is one family’s example, not a needed purchase. The authors also share music through singing and listening together.

entries.title: Watch a top turn
entries.summary: The appendix describes a pump-handle top that babies first enjoy following and may later learn to operate, with materials and parts suitable for their exploration.
entries.cue: Your baby follows a turning object or reaches toward its handle.
detail: The top’s movement can be interesting before the baby can make it spin. The authors describe a traditional tin top with a handle that pumps.
Their wider activity guidance allows watching and repeating. The activity can wait when it is frustrating or no longer holds interest.
